items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The container and wrapping of a product, which protects it and communicates information and brand image”.
items.answer: Packaging

items.stem: Explain how packaging can influence consumers’ perception of a product.
items.answer: Through sensory transference, features such as colour, shape and material create expectations of taste, quality or value that affect choice and even the experienced taste.

items.stem: Explain why manufacturers pay for products to be placed at eye level.
items.answer: Shoppers look at eye-level shelves first and longest, so products there are more likely to be noticed and bought.
items.markingKey: 1 mark attention; 1 mark purchase [2]

items.stem: A company in Kuala Lumpur is launching a new, strong-flavoured mint sweet and asks Hana to design the packaging. Suggest where in stores the sweets should be placed.
items.answer: At eye level or near checkouts, where impulse purchases are common.
items.markingKey: 1 mark position; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A company in Singapore is launching a new, strong-flavoured mint sweet and asks Daniel to design the packaging. (a) Suggest where in stores the sweets should be placed. (b) Explain one way to test whether the packaging works.
items.answer: (a) At eye level or near checkouts, where impulse purchases are common. (b) Show consumers both versions and ask them to rate expected intensity, or compare sales in stores using each design.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark position; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark method; 1 mark measure [2]

items.stem: “Becker et al.’s (2011) study of packaging and taste expectations has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including controls in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (controls): The packaging differed only in shape and colour saturation while the product was the same, so differences in ratings can be attributed to packaging. Strength (usefulness): Designers can use shape and colour to signal the intended taste. Weakness (generalisability): The study used one product type and one culture, so effects may differ for other products. Weakness (ecological validity): Participants rated packaging in a study rather than choosing products in a real store. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Explain the difference between brand loyalty and habitual buying.
items.answer: Brand loyalty involves repeat purchase plus a positive attitude and commitment to the brand; habitual buying is repeat purchase from convenience or inertia, so the consumer easily switches if something changes.

items.stem: Evaluate research on brand loyalty in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about supporting evidence.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Companies can use loyalty programmes and consistent branding to keep customers. Strength (supporting evidence): Blind taste tests show branded products are often preferred only when the brand is visible, showing the power of brand image. Weakness (cultural differences): Brand names may have different meanings or sounds in other languages. Weakness (measurement): Repeat purchase data cannot show whether buying is true loyalty or habit. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which packaging is more important than the product itself in influencing consumer choice. In your answer, you may refer to usefulness, ecological validity and individual differences.
items.answer: Arguments for: Packaging colour and shape affect expected taste (Becker et al., 2011). Eye-level shelf placement and attractive packs attract attention. items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Auty and Lewis’s (2004) study of product placement can be evaluated in terms of controls. Explain one strength of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Children saw the same clip with or without the brand, so the placement was the only difference.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to controls; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: After watching a film clip in Lima, children chose between two brands of cola. The table shows their choices. Saw the placement: chose the placed brand 32, chose the other brand 16; Saw the placement, older children: chose the placed brand 29, chose the other brand 22. Calculate the percentage of children for Saw the placement, older children that were “chose the placed brand”. Give your answer to one decimal place.

Daniel showed 8 children in Hanoi a film clip in which a brand of cola appeared and 8 children the same clip with the brand removed. Afterwards each child chose a drink, and the number choosing that brand over five occasions was recorded. Table: Times the brand was chosen (out of 5) — Placement clip: 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4. No-placement clip: 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 5. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) Calculate the median score for the no-placement clip condition. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that children who see the brand placed in a film clip will choose the placed brand more often than children who see the clip without the brand? Use the data in your answer. (d) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results.
items.answer: (a) IV: whether the film clip contained the product placement. DV: the number of occasions (out of 5) on which the child chose the placed brand. (b) 2 (c) Mean for placement clip = 3.1 and no-placement clip = 2.4; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 2 and 4) and the sample is small (n = 8 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (d) Use a larger sample with more participants in each condition, so that anomalous individuals have less effect and the results are more reliable and generalisable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) Ordered scores: 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5; median = 2. 1 mark: data ordered; 1 mark: correct median [2] (c) 1 mark: uses both means; 1 mark: judgement about direction; 1 mark: limitation such as overlap of scores, small sample or no statistical test [3] (d) 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how to do it; 1 mark: effect on validity/reliability explained [3]

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “The number of identical products displayed side by side at the front of a shelf”.
items.answer: Facings
items.markingKey: Facings: the number of identical products displayed side by side at the front of a shelf. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “End-of-aisle displays often increase sales.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how packaging can influence consumers’ perception of a product.
items.answer: (a) Correct. They are highly visible as shoppers turn into aisles. (b) Through sensory transference, features such as colour, shape and material create expectations of taste, quality or value that affect choice and even the experienced taste.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark sensory transference; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: Outline one weakness of Becker et al.’s (2011) study of packaging and taste expectations that relates to ecological validity.
items.answer: Participants rated packaging in a study rather than choosing products in a real store.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to ecological validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A company in Santiago is launching a new, strong-flavoured mint sweet and asks Lucas to design the packaging. Explain one way to test whether the packaging works.
items.answer: Show consumers both versions and ask them to rate expected intensity, or compare sales in stores using each design.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark measure [2]

items.stem: In a product placement study in Bangkok, children watched a film clip with or without a branded drink and then chose drinks on five occasions. Table: Times the brand was chosen (out of 5) — Placement clip: 4, 5, 2, 4, 3, 3. No-placement clip: 3, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2. Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study.
items.answer: IV: whether the film clip contained the product placement. DV: the number of occasions (out of 5) on which the child chose the placed brand.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2]

items.stem: In a product placement study in Nairobi, children watched a film clip with or without a branded drink and then chose drinks on five occasions. Table: Times the brand was chosen (out of 5) — Placement clip: 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 1. No-placement clip: 1, 0, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2. (a) Calculate the range of scores for each condition. (b) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Placement clip: 3; no-placement clip: 3. (b) The same drinks offered in the same positions.
items.markingKey: (a) Placement clip: 4 − 1 = 3; no-placement clip: 3 − 0 = 3. 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Dubai is interested in why consumers stay loyal to particular brands. Design an interview to test this. Your plan must include: one example question, the type of interview and how the data will be analysed.
items.answer: Method: an interview. A structured or semi-structured interview with set questions asked in the same order; record and transcribe answers; train interviewers. Variables: topic: reasons for brand loyalty; measure: rating scales and open answers. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Dubai, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: ‘Packaging is more important than the product itself in influencing consumer choice.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology. In your answer, you may refer to individual differences, usefulness and ecological validity.
items.answer: Arguments for: Packaging colour and shape affect expected taste (Becker et al., 2011). Eye-level shelf placement and attractive packs attract attention. Arguments against: Repeat purchases depend on product quality and brand loyalty. Price and recommendations from others also influence choice. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The idea that the sounds of a word suggest meanings, such as size or speed”?
items.answer: Sound symbolism
items.markingKey: Sound symbolism: the idea that the sounds of a word suggest meanings, such as size or speed. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how a brand name can influence consumers. (b) A student writes: “Brand loyalty can make consumers less sensitive to price rises.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) A meaningful or sound-symbolic name can suggest product qualities (speed, softness, strength), and a memorable name increases recognition and recall at the point of purchase. (b) Correct. Loyal consumers may continue to buy even when prices increase.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark meaning; 1 mark memorability [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “Brand loyalty can make consumers less sensitive to price rises.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Consumers choose brand names purely on how they sound.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Loyal consumers may continue to buy even when prices increase. (b) Not correct. Names work together with packaging, advertising, quality and price.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Freya showed 8 children in Singapore a film clip in which a brand of cola appeared and 8 children the same clip with the brand removed. Afterwards each child chose a drink, and the number choosing that brand over five occasions was recorded. Table: Times the brand was chosen (out of 5) — Placement clip: 4, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2, 3, 3. No-placement clip: 3, 2, 0, 3, 1, 2, 2, 4. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The placement clip condition had a higher mean (2.8) than the no-placement clip condition (2.1), suggesting that product placement increases children’s choice of the placed brand.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: Sofia showed 8 children in Jakarta a film clip in which a brand of cola appeared and 8 children the same clip with the brand removed. Afterwards each child chose a drink, and the number choosing that brand over five occasions was recorded. Table: Times the brand was chosen (out of 5) — Placement clip: 4, 4, 3, 4, 4, 5, 2, 2. No-placement clip: 3, 2, 0, 5, 4, 2, 3, 2. The participants were students whose names were drawn at random from a list of every student at a college in Jakarta. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: Random sampling. Weakness: it needs a complete list of the target population and selected people may refuse, so the final sample may still be unrepresentative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

items.stem: Omar showed 8 children in Karachi a film clip in which a brand of cola appeared and 8 children the same clip with the brand removed. Afterwards each child chose a drink, and the number choosing that brand over five occasions was recorded. Table: Times the brand was chosen (out of 5) — Placement clip: 3, 1, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2, 4. No-placement clip: 3, 3, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2. (a) Calculate the median score for the no-placement clip condition. (b) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 2 (b) The same film clip apart from the brand.
items.markingKey: (a) Ordered scores: 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3; median = 2. 1 mark: data ordered; 1 mark: correct median [2] (b) 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Seoul is interested in whether packaging colour affects how sweet people expect a drink to taste. Design a laboratory experiment to test this. Your plan must include: controls, the experimental design, the type of data collected and how the dependent variable will be measured.
items.answer: Method: a laboratory experiment. Manipulate the IV in a controlled room; standardised procedure and instructions; measure the DV objectively. Variables: IV: packaging colour; DV: expected sweetness rating (1–10). Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Seoul, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Define the term ‘implicit memory’.
items.answer: Memory that influences behaviour without conscious awareness.
items.markingKey: Implicit memory: memory that influences behaviour without conscious awareness. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “Product placement in children’s programmes raises ethical concerns.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Children may not understand the persuasive intent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of Auty and Lewis’s (2004) study of product placement in terms of ethics.
items.answer: Children were exposed to marketing for a sugary drink, and young children may not understand persuasive intent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to ethics; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: In a product placement study in Accra, children watched a film clip with or without a branded drink and then chose drinks on five occasions. Table: Times the brand was chosen (out of 5) — Placement clip: 3, 3, 4, 3, 2, 3. No-placement clip: 2, 2, 2, 1, 0, 3. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: Placement clip: 3.0; no-placement clip: 1.7.
items.markingKey: Placement clip: 18 ÷ 6 = 3.0; no-placement clip: 10 ÷ 6 = 1.7. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]
